claims.text: A conventional Cr-Mo low-alloy steel such as 4140 steel can exhibit a ductile–brittle–ductile transition under suitable tempering treatments.
The brittle intermediate state results from temporary embrittling species that dissolve or reconfigure at higher temperature.
The starting 4140 steel may be normalized or quenched and have a martensitic or bainitic microstructure.
A controlled tempering treatment in the 300–500 °C range can access the embrittling regime.
Subsequent heating above the embrittling regime can restore ductility.
Precise thermal profiles are required to produce a brief embrittlement phase followed by a more ductile state.
Phosphorus, antimony, or other alloying elements segregate to prior-austenite grain boundaries during tempering.
The segregated solutes re-dissolve or undergo other microstructural changes at higher temperatures.
Temperature-dependent grain-boundary solute segregation reduces grain-boundary cohesion in the intermediate temperature range.
Reduced grain-boundary cohesion causes temporary brittleness.
Further temperature increase mitigates the segregation-related mechanism and restores ductility.
The steel will lose ductility in the intermediate tempering range and recover it at higher temperatures.
Untempered or fully tempered steel with a stable microstructure will not exhibit the intermediate embrittlement step.
The transition depends on embrittling solutes such as P and Sb and on the heat-treatment conditions.
High-entropy alloys typically do not exhibit these transitions because they have reduced segregation and stable microstructures.
Transition temperatures and embrittlement severity vary with steel composition and tempering parameters.
